title: Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP): The Complete 2026 Guide
excerpt: A plain-English guide to the Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP): how much you can borrow, what it funds, who qualifies, what it costs, and how to apply through your bank.
content:
The Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP) is a federal loan-guarantee program, run by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), that helps for-profit Canadian businesses with $10 million or less in annual revenue borrow up to $1.15 million. You apply through a bank or credit union — not the government — and Ottawa shares the risk of loss with your lender so it can approve financing it might otherwise decline.

What is the Canada Small Business Financing Program?

The CSBFP is a loan-guarantee program created under the Canada Small Business Financing Act. The federal government does not lend the money itself. Instead, it partners with banks, credit unions and caisses populaires — who make and administer the loans — and reimburses them for a large share (currently about 85%) of eligible losses if a borrower defaults. That shared risk is what lets lenders say yes to younger or asset-light businesses that might not qualify for a conventional term loan.

The program has operated for decades and was designed to fill a specific gap: new and small firms often have solid plans but not enough collateral or track record to clear a bank's standard credit bar. The guarantee tips those borderline deals into approval. Thousands of CSBFP loans are registered across Canada each year, the large majority of them to small or newly established businesses.

The program is administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) at ised-isde.canada.ca. ISED sets the rules and registers each loan, but it never makes a lending decision or takes an application. Your financial institution does both, and nearly every major Canadian bank and credit union participates.

How much can you borrow through the CSBFP?

A borrower (together with any related borrowers) can access up to $1.15 million in total. That breaks down into a maximum of $1 million in term loans plus a separate $150,000 line of credit. Within the term-loan portion, sub-limits apply depending on what you are financing.

CategoryMaximum CSBFP amount (CAD)
Total per borrower (term loan + line of credit)$1,150,000
Term loans (all asset classes combined)$1,000,000
Real property (land and buildings)Up to $1,000,000
Equipment and leasehold improvementsUp to $500,000
Intangible assets and working capitalUp to $150,000 (within the $500,000)
Line of credit (working capital)$150,000

Real property is the only category that can draw on the full $1 million. Equipment and leasehold improvements share a $500,000 ceiling, and intangible assets plus working capital are capped at $150,000 within that amount. These sub-limits have been adjusted over the years, so confirm the current limit with your lender or the CSBFP website before you plan a large purchase.

One detail trips up groups of companies: the limits apply across "related borrowers," not just the single legal entity signing the loan. If you own several businesses that are financially or operationally connected, their combined CSBFP borrowing counts against the same $1.15 million ceiling unless they meet the program's test for being genuinely independent. If that could apply to you, raise it with your lender early so the structure is right from the start.

What can a CSBFP loan pay for — and what can't it?

CSBFP term loans are built for fixed and tangible assets. Eligible costs include purchasing or improving commercial real property, buying new or used equipment, financing new or existing leasehold improvements, certain intangible assets, working capital, and the program's 2% registration fee. A CSBFP line of credit covers day-to-day working capital and that registration fee.

The program will not finance everything. You generally cannot use a CSBFP loan to buy the shares of a business, to cover goodwill on its own, to refinance or pay down existing debt, or to fund assets held purely for investment. If you are buying an existing business, the loan is limited to the lesser of the purchase price or the appraised value of the eligible assets. The official exclusion list is longer than this, so ask your lender whether your specific cost qualifies.

If your main need is a single machine, vehicle or piece of kit, it is worth comparing the CSBFP route with dedicated equipment financing, where approval can be faster and the structure simpler.

Who is eligible for a CSBFP loan?

Most for-profit small businesses operating in Canada qualify, as long as gross annual revenue is $10 million or less in the fiscal year the loan is approved. Start-ups are eligible — you do not need years of history — and corporations, sole proprietorships, partnerships and co-operatives can all apply. Not-for-profit and charitable organizations are also eligible under the current rules.

The main exclusions are farming businesses, which have a separate program (the Canadian Agricultural Loans Act program), and any business above the $10 million revenue ceiling. The business must be carried on, or about to be carried on, for profit in Canada.

What does a CSBFP loan cost?

Two costs are specific to the program: a one-time registration fee and capped interest rates. The registration fee is 2% of the total loan amount, and it can be rolled into the loan rather than paid up front. Interest rates are capped, but your lender can always charge less than the ceiling.

ProductMaximum interest rate
Term loan — variableLender's prime rate + 3%
Term loan — fixedLender's residential mortgage rate + 3%
Line of creditPrime rate + 5%

These ceilings already include a 1.25% annual administration fee that the lender passes to the government. Your bank may also charge the ordinary set-up, renewal or management fees it applies to conventional loans; those are paid directly to the lender and cannot be financed into the CSBFP loan. The maximum government coverage period is 15 years for a term loan and 5 years for a line of credit.

Is the CSBFP a grant or a loan?

It is a loan, not a grant — you repay every dollar with interest. The "government" part is the guarantee working behind the scenes, which lowers the lender's risk rather than reducing what you owe. If you are specifically hunting for non-repayable funding, the CSBFP is not it; look instead at federal and provincial grant and contribution programs. The upside of a loan is that there is no competitive application window and no requirement to match funds the way many grants demand.

How do you apply for a CSBFP loan?

You apply directly to a participating financial institution — a bank, credit union or caisse populaire — not to the government. The lender reviews your application against its usual credit criteria, decides whether to approve it, and then registers the loan with ISED. Because each institution chooses which deals to put through the program, it pays to approach more than one lender.

That is where a matching service saves time. Instead of booking appointments one bank at a time, you can get matched with a lender through our quick loan estimator, then raise the CSBFP in your conversation. See how it works for the full process, and read our broader guide to small business loans in Canada if you are weighing several financing options at once.

Is the CSBFP right for your business?

The CSBFP is strongest when you need to finance fixed assets — property, equipment, renovations — and you are a newer or smaller business a conventional lender would hesitate to fund. The trade-offs are the 2% registration fee, the restriction to eligible asset classes, and a process that can take longer than a private lender's. If you need fast, flexible working capital or want to borrow against receivables, a private term loan or another product may fit better. For a side-by-side look at a popular alternative, see our comparison of the CSBFP versus a BDC loan.

A simple way to decide: list what you actually need to buy and how quickly. If it is a building, a fit-out or heavy equipment and you can wait a few weeks for a bank decision, the CSBFP's capped rates and generous terms are hard to beat. If it is working capital you need next week, or the purchase falls outside the eligible asset classes, keep the program on your shortlist but line up alternatives at the same time so you are not left waiting.

Frequently asked questions

Does the government lend the money directly?

No. The CSBFP is a loan guarantee, not a direct loan. Banks, credit unions and caisses populaires provide the funds and administer the loan; ISED registers it and reimburses the lender for most eligible losses if the loan defaults.

What is the maximum CSBFP loan?

Up to $1.15 million per borrower — $1 million in term loans plus a $150,000 line of credit. Sub-limits apply by asset class, and real property is the only category that can use the full $1 million. Confirm the current limits with your lender or the CSBFP website.

Can a start-up get a CSBFP loan?

Yes. Start-ups are eligible as long as the business operates for profit in Canada and has (or expects) $10 million or less in gross annual revenue. You still need to satisfy the lender's own credit assessment.

What interest rate will I pay?

Rates are capped at prime + 3% for a variable term loan, the residential mortgage rate + 3% for a fixed term loan, and prime + 5% for a line of credit. Many lenders charge below the cap, so your actual rate depends on your credit profile and your lender.

How long does CSBFP approval take?

It varies by lender, because the bank runs its normal underwriting before registering the loan. It is usually slower than an online private lender but faster than many government grants. Approaching more than one participating lender can shorten the wait.

Can I use a CSBFP loan to buy an existing business?

Partly. You can finance eligible assets of the business — equipment, real property, leasehold improvements — up to the lesser of the purchase price or their appraised value, but you cannot use the loan to buy the company's shares or goodwill on its own.
